title: Burst pipe? What to do in the first five minutes
excerpt: Find the stop valve, kill the power to anything wet, and open a cold tap. Here's the order that saves the most damage.
content:
A burst pipe can put hundreds of gallons on the floor in an hour. What you do before we arrive decides how much of it ends up in the ceiling below. Do these in order.

1. Turn off the water

Find the main stop valve. In most homes it's under the kitchen sink or in the basement where the water pipe comes through the wall. Turn it clockwise until it stops. If it's stuck, don't force it with a wrench: call us and we'll talk you through the outside shut-off.

2. Make it safe

If water is near sockets, lights or an electric water heater, switch those circuits off at the breaker panel. Don't stand in water to do it.

3. Drain the system

Open the cold taps on the lowest floor and flush the toilets. That empties the pipes so less water escapes from the break.

4. Save what you can

  • Move furniture and rugs out of the way
  • Put buckets under drips and poke a small hole in a bulging ceiling so it drains into a bucket, not across the room
  • Take photos for your insurer before you start mopping

5. Call us

We answer day and night: 555 0142. Most of the county gets a plumber within the hour.

title: Five signs your water heater is about to give up
excerpt: Rusty water, popping noises and a puddle at the base: what each one means, and when a repair still makes sense.
content:
Most tank water heaters last eight to twelve years. They rarely die without warning. Here's what to look and listen for.

  1. Rusty or brown hot water. The tank may be rusting from the inside, usually because the anode rod has worn away.
  2. Popping or rumbling. Sediment has built up on the bottom. A flush can help if it isn't too late.
  3. Water around the base. Check the valve and fittings first; if the tank itself is weeping, it needs replacing.
  4. Hot water runs out faster. A failed element or a tank full of sediment.
  5. It's over ten years old. Look for the date on the label. Plan a replacement before it floods the basement.

Repair or replace?

If the heater is under eight years old and the tank isn't leaking, a repair is usually worth it. Over ten years, with rust or a leak, put the money towards a new one: it'll cost less to run, too.

Not sure? Ask for a free quote and we'll tell you straight.

title: Why grease is the drain's worst enemy
excerpt: Hot fat runs down easily and sets like candle wax in the pipe. Here's what to do with it instead.
content:
Half the blocked kitchen drains we clear are grease. It goes down hot and runny, then cools in the pipe and sets, catching food scraps until nothing gets past.

What to do instead

  • Pour cooled fat into an old jar or can and put it in the trash
  • Wipe greasy pans with a paper towel before washing them
  • Use a sink strainer and empty it into the trash
  • Once a week, run the hot tap for a minute after washing up

What not to do

Skip the chemical drain cleaners. They rarely shift a real grease block, they're hard on old pipes, and they're dangerous for whoever opens the pipe next.

If the sink is draining slowly, we can clear it and camera-check the pipe so it stays clear.

title: Get your heating ready before the first cold snap
excerpt: Bleed the radiators, check the pressure and book the yearly service now, before everyone else does.
content:
Every year the first cold week brings a rush of calls about boilers that haven't run since spring. Twenty minutes now saves a cold night later.

  1. Turn the heating on for an hour and check every radiator warms up
  2. Bleed any radiator that's cold at the top
  3. Check the boiler pressure gauge: most should read between 1 and 1.5 bar when cold
  4. Test your carbon monoxide alarm
  5. Insulate pipes in the garage, crawl space and attic
